anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects or re-uses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, inflating the cost of individual statements.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer is unable to supply the required read/write bandwidth or latency, so database requests accumulate in the I/O subsystem.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: poorly chosen plans perform large table scans, Cartesian joins, or serial executions that issue many more logical and physical I/Os than a good plan would. The excessive I/O meets an already saturated storage layer, so each physical read or write is delayed. Statements therefore hold row, key-range, or table locks for far longer, lengthening blocking chains. Waiting sessions pile up behind both locks and I/O, driving transaction response times to spike, connection pools to exhaust, and deadlock detectors to fire. Performance metrics show a mixture of high lock-wait time, high I/O wait time, low CPU utilization, erratic plan changes in the cache, and sudden throughput collapses that are difficult to attribute to a single subsystem.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan is the initiating amplifier: it multiplies the amount of data touched and the duration locks are held. The longer lock hold times increase the probability and depth of lock contention. In turn, blocked transactions remain active and continue to issue or retry I/O requests, further stressing the storage layer and aggravating the I/O throughput anomaly. The storage bottleneck feeds back by slowing every I/O-bound statement, which stretches lock lifetimes even more and gives the optimizer more chances to pick or reuse bad plans under changing cache and parameter conditions. The intertwined feedback loops between inefficient plans, prolonged lock contention, and saturated storage create a self-reinforcing degradation that can bring an OLTP system to a standstill unless all three root causes are addressed together.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
